utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I would explain that yesterday that there was no chance of resuming since one of the standard rules in the case of emergencies, and there was a little fire problem, as I understand yesterday, is that the accused are returned to the United Nations Detention Unit, and there was no reasonable option to have him transported back in time. Communication on my part that we would not continue could have been better. I put that on the record. Then, Mr. McCloskey, perhaps we could already have the witness escorted into the courtroom. The Chamber was informed that the Office of the Prosecutor has received -- has received a revised English translation for P2109, and we dealt with that document, and that's 65 ter 05816. We dealt with it on the 4th of September and that the document -- that is that the revised English translation is now uploaded into e-court under doc ID 04257966-ET-1, and that the Prosecution would like that the new revised English translation replaces the old one. This is confirmed. Madam Registrar, could you please replace the old translation by the new one, and it's not me who has all these numbers on his mind but I was just reading from an e-mail that was sent in anticipation of this by Ms. Stewart. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for saving me from doing that. The revised translation is something that both parties have agreed with as well, as you know there was some concern by the Defence. So that issue is done with. The document itself, in speaking to Mr. Ivetic, I believe there is still an objection to it. As it's still MFI'd, and as you may recall this was the 11 July document in General Mladic's name where he had shown concern about the 28th Division coming or elements of the 28th Division coming back from Sarajevo to assist in the Srebrenica front. And we had a document that was a bit different than our normal -- what we -- teletypes that we see and that was part of the objection that Mr. Ivetic made. So we went into our collection and we did find three original teletypes of the document that came from the Drina Corps collection and went to various units. We do have those, if you wish to see them, but we would again try to offer the Banja Luka archive document into evidence but I will also offer one of the others so that's in evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask first, Mr. Ivetic, whether the objection stands, in view of the fact that there are various copies of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, and if I can just briefly explain that. The other documents are teletexts that would be received and they have the printed SR, "Svojom Rukom," or "by one's hand," on the form which is what would be expected if an original signed by commander were sent through the teletext transmission system. The purported original from the Banja Luka archives bears a stamp as if it were the original, and has SR handwritten on the end showing that it's not a -- one that's received from the -- via the teletext system and has no signature. So that leads us to questions about the authenticity of this document given that it does not follow the protocol that would have been followed that someone had to sign the original, stamp it, and then give it to the teletext operator to send it via the teletext transmission system, and therefore we don't know at this stage why that document is the way it is and we have to maintain our objection. So that's in essence our position on that document, and I again stress that the SR on the original -- on the original one that's in e-court is handwritten whereas on the others it's all teletyped, meaning that this handwritten document without a signature is what purports to be the original that would have been sent and it's not signed, which, of course, that doesn't happen with other documents from the -- purportedly from the Main Staff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any further submissions on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document that counsel has referred to. We are not suggesting that it is the original. We got it from the Banja Luka archives, from the RS government. It is a typed document but I believe what Mr. Ivetic is referring to a handwritten SR is, as you can see from the one in the computer, but I can look at it. It appears to me to be some kind of copy or photocopy so we are not precisely sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- of the origin of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would like to have a look at it and we will then decide on whether to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I will pass you up 65 ter 25760 which is one of the three teletype originals that we believe is the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that there is no dispute about the document on the receiver side having SR typewritten there, whatever that may mean. So therefore, if it's uploaded -- I think if there is no dispute about that, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there it also no dispute that it was received as such, whether there was ever an original signed or not but that it was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be. I believe there is three or maybe even four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- separate units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that that text was received by the recipient is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we don't need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt, Mr. McCloskey, can I please repeat the 65 ter number that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that into evidence as well just so we have two. That will help with the confusion, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there is no dispute about -- there seems to be dispute about the version that was found in the Banja Luka archives and there is no dispute about this text having been received by three or -- addressees on the other side with Ratko Mladic SR typewritten at the bottom. So therefore, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'd like to remind you again that you're bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and apologies for continuing with our own conversations when you entered the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, I think if I look at the various clocks and if I remember that you asked for ten hours, then that would mean that approximately by the end of this day you would have concluded your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's roughly our addition as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then get started as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And yes, if we -- and if we will recall, Mr. Butler, when the alarm went off, was right in the middle of responding to Judge Moloto's questions and if I can just help reiterate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was -- basically we had seen a document which is 65 ter 1927. I believe it was on our screen and this was the Mladic order ordering a communications person to go to General Milovanovic in the Krajina, and it had an SR next to it, and not --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is now P2125.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And a few documents before that, we had P2122, which was a very similar document, where General Mladic had announced the power failure at Veliki Zep, and that document in General Mladic's name, did not have an SR on it. So I think the guts of the question was: Do you have an explanation for why we see one document regarding a comms person to Milovanovic with an SR on it and we have another comms outage document without an SR on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just correct that, my question. My question was not to ask for an explanation why we do have that. My question was: Do you know what the difference is between those two types of situations? And can you tell us what it is, if you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, as both the Prosecution and Defence have noted, there is a technical difference between a document that has an SR and one that does not. My view is that, functionally, there is no particular difference within the context of the fact that how these orders would be taken by subordinate commands. Again, as I believe I was discussing yesterday before the alarm went off, the VRS is a -- or at least certainly at the staff level is a professionally trained army with well-educated and competent officers who knew the limits of their authorities. So when one looks at orders like this, that are received with a signature block of General Mladic on them, or any other authorised superior, how they follow those orders is not going to matter whether there is an SR and that General Mladic has personally signed this order or it goes off under his signature block. It will be treated in the exact same way as it is militarily proper to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thank you very much for that answer and I do understand what you are saying. I guess what I really do want to find out is notwithstanding the fact that subordinate organs would follow the order irrespective of whether it's got an SR or not, do you by any chance know procedurally within the Main Staff what the meaning or what the difference in meaning between the document with an SR is as against a document without an SR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't -- I'm sure some individuals may have testified in that regard. I do not know how the Main Staff itself would have qualified that, for example, whether if General Mladic relayed it telephonically that would still qualify for an SR designation versus whether or not the order was actually hand drafted by him or whether or not he simply personally signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On that same topic, Mr. Butler, let me read to you something to see if it -- your response to it. It comes from the Tolimir transcript, page 110511, and I'm asking General Keserovic -- remind us who Keserovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of July 1995, he is Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic who is a security officer on the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I put up a document signed by General Mladic and I ask: "Well, seeing how the document is not signed by General Mladic, the one on the screen, it must have also been sent somehow via teletype. I don't -- I can't think of any other" -- sorry, this is an answer. "... I can't think of any other reason why it wouldn't be signed." "Q. Okay. Down in the left corner of this original document we can see next to Ratko Mladic's name, 'S.R.' Tell us what that means." And the answer of Keserovic is: "When a document is submitted to signalsmen to be sent by teletype or other communication, during the handover, because the signature cannot be conveyed by teletype, these letters, 'S.R.,' meaning 'in his own hand,' are inserted to indicate that the original document was signed by General Mladic." How does that fit your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean that is consistent. I would add, for example, for the Court to note, that many of the documents, I mean we will see them actually as documents that are handwritten, but as you will recall from some of the earlier Bratunac documents, military orders might very well be written out long hand in certain cases and then relayed for typing and publication later down the line. The fact that an officer may have handwritten a document like that and signed it, when that order is typed, he's not available to do that, it may very well also get the SR designation reflecting it is in the commander's hand. So again, obviously without seeing a physical signature on a document, I cannot say whether or not he actually signed that document but there are a variety of methods obviously that the personal nature of the order, from a superior to a subordinate, can be relayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1309. We are on the 14th of July in our chronology. This is an intercept where the date of the intercept is noted in P01311 but let's stick with P1309, which was on our exhibit list for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we will see that this is at 2102 hours, between the Palma duty officer Major Jokic and Badem. Can you remind us what Palma and Badem are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that we dealt with that, Mr. McCloskey, and that we even asked whether there was any dispute about it? And there was no dispute about it? And it's even adjudicated facts, if I remember well. I don't remember whether there was any objection to that adjudicated fact but let's try to keep things as succinct as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I merely do it to remind you of who these people are. I forget these things easily. If you know who they are and there is no problem, I won't, but I just want to make sure you remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we do. Otherwise we will ask for it, if we have problems, and sometimes we look it up because I know that Palma was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right. We just dealt with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Butler, so we see that this is between Badem and Palma duty officer Major Jokic, and who is Major Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Jokic by position is the chief of engineering services for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, and I won't read it all but we see here that Major Jokic is calling Bratunac to look for -- looking for Beara and notes in that first part on the fourth line in the English, the higher house urgently needs him and then as we go down we see that he actually speaks to Colonel Beara and is telling him that 155 had called him and he needs to call them back. Can you tell us, in your view, what the higher house means and what 155 is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this context, the higher house is the Main Staff, and telephone number 155 is actually the extension to the office of the chief of operations of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the operations centre, I should say, of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And almost two-thirds down the page, Jokic says: "Yes, hey, we have huge problems over here" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we still on the right page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's B/C/S page 2. Thank you. I had that in my note. I just missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Jokic, after saying "we have huge problems over here," then says: "There are big problems, well, with the people, I mean the parcel." What do you believe that means? The problems, first of all, and then this reference to parcel and people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in this context, there could only be two groups of people that the Zvornik Brigade is dealing with at the time. One particular group obviously at this point of time on 14 July is the column of individuals that is transversing now through the rear area of the Zvornik Brigade. The other group of people is the prisoners that are being held in schools in various locations, given the fact that at first the individual corresponding is Colonel Beara and there is another reference to Drago, who I believe is Drago Nikolic, the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade. I take it in this context that they are discussing the issue of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you aware from the documents or materials any problems with prisoners in the Zvornik area on the evening of 14 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Problems in the sense that there are prisoners in -- I mean, one there are prisoners in various locations already, and temporally, by this time at 2100 hours, on 14 July 1995, they are still -- the engineers are still working to bury the individuals who were killed at Orahovac and, several hours in the future, the executions will begin of those prisoners that are being held at the school in Petkovci. Because of the security situation in and around the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, many of the convoys of prisoners who are going further to the north, for example, to locations such as Rocevic and Pilica, are being stopped and held in temporary locations because the roads are no longer secure. And in fact on this evening, there is witnesses who talk about the fact that two busloads of prisoners are actually stuck and stranded in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade compound because it's not safe for them to continue to move at night because of the unclear military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to 15 July, P1319. And Mr. Butler, this is an intercept that says Colonel Beara was looking for General Zivanovic but he was not there. He said he was to call him at extension 139. Do you know what date this occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is 15 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now we see that. It speaks for itself but do you -- have you identified what extension 139 is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Extension 139 is the phone in the office of Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, the chief of security for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you determine that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of not only the records seized in Zvornik but other documents that we have acquired through the years, one of them was a phonebook. Looking at those particular documents, it notes the fact that extension 139 at the Zvornik Brigade is for the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you then checked whether that number is or at least the person attached to that number is consistent with the content of the telephone conversations? I mean you find in the phonebook a number, it's attached to an office of someone. Now, that can be right or wrong. One of the ways of verifying is to look at the content of the telephone conversations whenever any reference is made to 193, or whatever the number is, and then to verify whether that is consistent or logical with being attached to the person you found in the phonebook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir, and particularly in this context, I believe and I certainly am aware that in other cases or trials, witness testimony has been led that reflects Colonel Beara was at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters during this period, so it would be logical that he would be using the office of the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade as a focal point where people could reach him telephonically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go to P1320. This is an intercept on the same day, two minutes later from the last one, at 954 hours. And the participants are General Zivanovic and Colonel Ljubo Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be clear, on all these transcripts of intercepted telephone conversations, Madam Registrar is cautious enough to take care that they will not be broadcast because they are all under seal. Second, they are all MFIed. So just to remind the parties of that. The Chamber still has to decide on the whole -- yes, I think they were conditionally admitted but we will have a closer look at it, but they are not -- it's not just plain evidence as with most of the admitted documents. Just to remind the parties of the status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My reminder is now behind me and so that is very helpful that we just keep all those documents under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Butler, this intercept, we see, a conversation laid out between Zivanovic, the commander of the Drina Corps and Colonel Beara. And as we get down in the English, Beara says: "I informed the commander of this, Furtula did not send Lukic's Intervention Platoon the other day." Can you tell us -- remind us who Furtula is and who you think this Lukic is and his Intervention Platoon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Furtula, Major Furtula is the commander of the Visegrad Light Infantry Brigade. Lukic in this context is one of his platoon or company commanders, an individual that I believe is known as Milan Lukic who is well known for his activities in the Visegrad area in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so just tell us briefly what this -- well, tell us, "I informed the commander of this," when Beara is making that reference, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context, Beara's commander would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you read the rest of this intercept, just tell us briefly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In short, this is a conversation between Colonel Beara and General Zivanovic where Colonel Beara is essentially requesting General Zivanovic make available resources or to facilitate more quick transfer of these individuals from the Visegrad Brigade in order to follow the orders that were given. General Zivanovic at this time is no longer the corps commander of the Drina Corps having been relieved of his duties of that on 13 July 1995. So what General Zivanovic is saying clearly is that he's no longer authorised to give such instructions and he instructs Colonel Beara to call a certain extension where he can reach the new corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so when Beara says, "he simply does not heed what the commanders orders him," again what reference -- who is the commander in that reference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in that particular context, we are talking about Colonel Beara noting that the commander of the Visegrad Brigade has failed to follow the orders of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can read the rest of that. Let's go to the next page in English. And we see that Zivanovic says: "I can no longer decide this." Explain that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did earlier. General Zivanovic is no longer the commander of the Drina Corps. He no longer has the authorisation to be able to make those kind of orders relating to units that are no longer subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we can see, as we go down, Zivanovic repeatedly mentions 385 and then says: "Zlatar and 385." So Zlatar and 385 is what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatar is the Drina Corps headquarters. 385 is the phone extension that is reserved for the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And but on the 15th, where would the commander of the Drina Corps, at this time, as we know, it's General Krstic, where would he be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be in the field with Drina Corps units that are involved in operations around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how does the 385 extension fit, if Krstic is in the field in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, both from my awareness of the investigation as well as the prior testimony of the Drina Corps chief of communications, he discussed the fact that 385 was the designated number and through switchboards and other communication means, that number followed the commander wherever he was. So all somebody had to do, if you -- no matter where the corps commander was, his phone number was 385, whether he happened to be in Zepa, whether he happened to be back at Vlasenica, it was set up so that it was always possible to reach the commander regardless of where you were calling from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next intercept, 21008A. This is a 15 July intercept, just a few minutes after the last one, this one is noted at 1000 hours, and the participants are noted, Colonel Ljubo Beara and General Krstic. Do you relate this intercept in any way to the last one we just heard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's directly related both in the sense of immediately following in time, as well as related within the context of they are discussing the same matter, this time Colonel Beara is discussing it with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this time we see in the first line, Beara says: "General, Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order." In that context, we now have this term "boss" is used. Who do you believe Beara is referring to when he said "boss's order"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he's referring to General Mladic. It would not make sense if the order were given by, say, General Krstic or General Zivanovic, Ljubo Beara would be more appropriately saying, "they didn't follow your order." The fact that he's saying "the boss's order" infers strongly that they are referring about General Mladic. The boss of both Colonel Beara and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then, we see he's still asking for 30 men, as it was ordered, and from this, who ordered the 30 men, in your view? It says: "But I need 30 men, just like it was ordered."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, again in that context, the person -- you know, it was ordered. There apparently was an order issued by the individual known as -- referred to as the boss for at least a platoon of men for a certain task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you read the rest of this and from your knowledge of it, what do you believe the certain task was that Beara was requesting those men pursuant to Mladic's order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading this particular intercept, as well as the context of other things that were happening, on the ground at that time, this particular task that they are talking about and the men that they needed were those men who would carry out the executions of prisoners in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We will get into a bit of the detail to find out how it is that you come to that conclusion. But before we get there I'd like to continue down the intercept. When Krstic says, "Take them from Nastic or Blagojevic," remind us who Nastic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nastic is the commander of the Milici Light Infantry Brigade. Blagojevic is the commander of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the next line, Beara says: "But I don't have any here, I need them today, and I'll give them back tonight. Krle, you have to understand, I can't explain it to you like this." What's Krle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krle is a nickname for General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Krstic says: "I'll disturb everything on his axis if I pull them out and a lot depends on him." What do you believe he's referring to, disturbing his axis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in the context of the time when this discussion is occurring, General Krstic is already dealing with the situation at Zepa. He has just released within the past several hours equivalent of two task forces or two light battalions of soldiers from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade from the Zepa battlefield area where they were engaged to return back to Zvornik to deal with the military threat of the column. So at this point he's being expected to continue military operations towards Zepa and he's just lost a significant percentage of the combat forces that he was using to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so? Who do he lose?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He last Colonel Pandurevic and he lost the two battle groups from the Zvornik Brigade that were sent from Zepa back to Zvornik on the morning hours of 15 July 1995. Because of the threat of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Beara says: "I can't resolve anything without 15 to 30 men, and that Boban Indjic" -- this is the first mention we here of Boban Indjic. Did you determine who he is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Boban Indjic is a subordinate to Milan Lukic and is also somebody who is known notoriously for his activities in Visegrad in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you find an intercept that made reference, some reference on the 13th of July, to Boban Indjic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a prior intercept on the 13th which reflects the fact that a busload of soldiers from Visegrad was proceeding north and broke down, and as a result, the soldiers went back or could not move any further forward. So what you have happening is it wasn't exactly that Major Furtula did not follow the boss's order, he did try and follow the boss's order but because of a mechanical issue, the platoon of soldiers that were supposed to do this was stranded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Krstic says: "Ljubo, this is not protected." Is he referring to the open airways that they are speaking over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Beara says: "I know, I know." And then Krstic says: "I'll see what I can do but it will disturb a lot. Have a look down there at Nastic and Blagojevic's." Then Beara says: "But I don't have any, if I did I wouldn't still be asking for the third day." And I think we can do the subtracting on that to determine when he was asking originally. And then Krstic says: "Check with Blagojevic, take his Red Berets." Who are the Red Berets of Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Beret unit was an intervention unit of the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade consisting of young and fit soldiers. The unit for the most part -- or all of the members of the unit, I think, except three or four essentially deserted the army on the morning of 15 July 1995 or the late evening of the 14th of July 1995, because most of them were reserve police officers and they actually, without authorisation, left the army and put themselves at the disposal of Dragan Vasic in order to become police officers in the town of Srebrenica as he was standing up the police station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents later that, of course, we seized from the Bratunac Brigade where it discusses the very fact that most of the individuals of the unit deserted the army at a certain point of time and they are now employed as police officers in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Krstic goes on and says: "I'll see what I can do." Beara says: "Check it out and have them go to Drago's." Who do you take Drago to be here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, Drago's is a reference to Drago Nikolic, chief of security of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why would he have them go to Drago's? Where would that be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prisoners were being held at that time in schools throughout the municipality of the Zvornik area. Drago Nikolic was an individual who was involved in the holding and the execution and the events afterwards with the prisoners. He would be the logical person in this particular context to send these people to so then Nikolic could give them further orders on where they needed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Krstic says: "I can't guarantee anything." Beara says: "Krle, I don't know what to do anymore." And Krstic says: "Ljubo, take those MUP men from up there." And then Beara says: "No, they won't do anything." What do you believe that reference to the MUP men that won't do anything is? As he says on -- he says: "I talked, there is no other solution but for the 15 to 30 men from Indjic." Who are the MUP men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again in context of what is happening in Zvornik at the time, a number of MUP forces, police forces, have been sent to the Zvornik Brigade area to reinforce against the threat of the column. In the context of this discussion, Colonel Beara sounds as he has inquired as to whether or not they would be willing to participate in the executions and whoever was the commander of those particular MUP units declined. Colonel Beara as an army individual would not necessarily have the authority to order the MUP to do this type of a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we see for the next couple of lines they go on with just comments of frustration about this issue. Krstic says: "Fuck it, now I'll be the one to blame." Beara says: "I don't know what to do. I mean, Krle, there are still 3500 parcels that I have to distribute and I have no solution." What do you take this to mean, "there are still 3500 parcels to deliver and I have no solution"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take this to mean that at this point in time, Colonel Beara understands or believes that there are still 3500 prisoners that he has to deal with, deal with meaning execute, and that he has no ability to conduct these executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from the documents in the investigation, can you tell us, does -- how does this fit into it? This number of 3500?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's probably at this point in time a little high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time this conversation takes place, again in context of what we know happened on the ground, the prisoners at Orahovac, which numbered between 800 and a thousand, I believe are the generally accepted estimates, are already dead. The prisoners that were held at the school in Petkovci, and again between 800 and a thousand are numbers that I'm familiar with, there also their executions have just been completed and the engineers are working to bury the bodies at the foot of the dam. There are still a group of prisoners, a large group of prisoners, and again, I'm not sure of the exact numbers at the school at Rocevic that have not yet been started to be executed. There is a large group of prisoners at the school in Kula who have not yet begun to have been executed. And again, as the information that I'm aware of notes, once the school in Kula was full, they started putting the overflow prisoners in the Dom of Culture in the village of Pilica. So again, if one uses as a baseline figure a thousand prisoners per school location, that's 4.000. Perhaps another 5.000 [sic] in the Dom of Culture. Already 2.000 of the prisoners are dead. He really only has to dispose of or execute another 2500, not 3500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this term "parcels," we have just saw that term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you said: "Perhaps another 5.000 in the Dom of Culture." Did you mean another thousand which makes a total of 5.000 or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe I said another 500 in the Dom of Culture, I hope I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that clarifies it. I think you said 5.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see this term "parcels" used by Beara. We just heard the term or saw the term "parcels" used by Jokic. How do you take -- do you see this term "parcels" used in other contexts to determine -- to refer to the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That phrase is used in the context to refer to the Muslim prisoners in a number of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Jokic's slip of the tongue when he said, "people, I mean parcels," assist in that analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, but again, one of the reasons why in our own communications security protocols we tell people not to talk around sensitive topics on an open line is because even though you think you're disguising what may be happening at the time, with the benefit of hindsight it -- obviously to any opponent it becomes evidently clear what you were talking about. The fact that Colonel Jokic himself -- or Major Jokic at the time himself compromised that does lend assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see "parcels" also on the semi-last line on this page but then in quotation marks. Now, I wonder, is that in the original? And how can you hear quotation marks if it's an intercepted telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I said "hear" that was a mistake, Mr. President. These are not audios.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, let me see. I'll have a look at the -- I'll have a look at the -- yes, I see that it appears in the original as well, "paketa" which is in quotation marks. Nevertheless, this is written down by someone who listened in, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So still, whether it's audio recorded or not, you still need someone to hear quotation marks. Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I would suggest that that would be a question for the individual to explain his methodology in doing this as part of their processing. It's not a question I can answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P1497, we are still on the 15th of July. We will skip ahead, Mr. Butler, from the issues of Milovanovic -- Milanovic and others. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, one of my colleagues draws my attention to the fact that you introduced this report under its 65 ter number. Do you want to tender it or is it already MFI'd? Has it received a number already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just confused where we are. Which one? An intercept or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is -- has that received already a number, an exhibit number, whether or not MFI'd? No, not. Madam Registrar says it has not. Therefore, the Chamber wonders whether you want to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please, and thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object to this intercept as we have the others related to the authenticity of the same. We believe this witness in opining as to what he believes that the document means and what the events in question are is a self-fulfilling prophecy and cannot be used to self-authenticate these intercepts for which, as Your Honours have seen, there are some questions of how quotation marks could have been transmitted or heard by an operator, whether listening to the conversation live or via an audio recording. So we would object to the introduction of this document on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar? The number to be assigned would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21008A receives number P2126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, a version of this intercept is in evidence and I have just inadvertently used the one that wasn't and I will find that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that in evidence or is it also conditionally admitted? Is it one in the series?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give the number then we will further verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we will dig that up for you and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but important is that should we vacate number P2126?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would not. It's the -- I probably -- it's the nice print-out with the clear date on it and, as you know, there has been some confusion there. So I think this -- this is a good one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we leave it as it is and you'll inform us under what number the other version of the same intercept is known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we are at P1497 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it is 10.30 by now. If you have only half a question on this, then we would hear it. If you have more, we would like to take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have more. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it looks as if the witness is ready to further be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's go to P1497, it's there, I see it. And this is an interim combat report. We see in the name -- if we go to the second page in English, it's signed by Vinko Pandurevic. And if you go up a little bit in the Serbian so we can see the bottom of that so we actually see a signature, is this an original copy that we got from the Zvornik Brigade from that search?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, is, it is. The original version of this exists in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we are now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or I should say more appropriately in the evidence vault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We are now, as we can see, in the evening hours from the stamp of 1925 hours, that it was -- looks like a sent to the Drina Corps, and we do recall that you just testified about Vinko Pandurevic's units coming back from the Zepa operation to help deal with the problem of the approaching column, which you have talked about so I don't want you to get into that in detail, but these first three paragraphs, can you -- we see that it's just a discussion of the very difficult defence posture that the Zvornik Brigade is in. Is that correct? Could you just offer us your brief words on these first three big paragraphs that Pandurevic is giving to his command up above the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, again in context, on the morning of 15 July 1995, Colonel Pandurevic and the Zvornik Brigade forces that were currently engaged in military operations in Zepa were sent back to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade in order to deal with the deteriorating military situation in that zone as a result of the column. These three paragraphs, the first three paragraphs of this document, lay out the tactical understanding of the situation that Colonel Pandurevic has at that time and which he is trying to relay to his superior at the Drina Corps, in this case General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from your knowledge, are these -- the information in these three paragraphs roughly accurate as to the situation and his true perception of the situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To a degree it is accurate. Clearly it is deteriorating even as he is writing this so by the time the actual report is published at the headquarters of the [indiscernible], the situation is getting worse by the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to put it in overall context, as the Muslim -- armed head of the Muslim column came to this area of the Zvornik Brigade around Baljkovica and the 2nd Corps came across the lines in the early morning hour of the 16th, was that where the fierce fighting occurred and the casualties you've already spoken about occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the morning of the 16th July 1995, the column actually overran the battalion headquarters of the 4th Infantry Battalion near Baljkovica. Also at the same time, on the morning, they had lost an entire company of soldiers and police forces that had come in from various groups that had put out -- had actually been lost in the woods. Colonel Pandurevic at that time feared that that unit had been completely wiped out since it was lost and had no -- he had no radio communications with it. So he believed by the 16th, the morning of the 16th, he was heavily engaged and was taking heavy casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To clear that issue up, that unit was found later; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. It did emerge, it had just simply gotten lost in the night. It had no radio communications. Colonel Pandurevic and the Zvornik Brigade naturally under the circumstances assumed the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So now getting to the fourth paragraph, an additional -- and I quote: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain." Now, of course, the Trial Chamber is fully aware of the prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area. What do you take this term "obligations of security" to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original word in Serbo-Croatian is asanacija. If one looks it up in any of a number of JNA military lexicons or dictionaries, it refers to the process essentially of burying biological waste products that are created on the battlefield for health and safety reasons. The reality is it's a word used to describe, by the military, their burying of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you're referring to restoration of the terrain or obligations of security? I asked you about obligations of security.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise completely. I was one ahead there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obligations of security, I have testified previously, is Colonel Pandurevic's awareness of the requirement to guard the prisoners in these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we have seen security officers engaged in the implementation of the murder operation, but is it your understanding that the obligations of security in that context is a completely different word in Serbian so this does not mean the obligations of the security branch?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, so, and again in context of what's happening at this time, Colonel Pandurevic is aware that at the very minimum, his military police units are being used to have to guard the thousands of prisoners at the schools. And in fact, not only are military police units guarding them, other soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade who could be performing duties on the front line or in other locations are, in fact, also being pulled out of various locations in order to guard these prisoners because clearly a thousand desperate prisoners in a single location makes for a significant security threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you just mentioned the -- in the previous answer, the thousand plus in the area of the Kula school and the Pilica cultural centre. Are Pandurevic's people involved in guarding those?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Rocevic, Kozluk, the executions that occurred that day, is it clear whether or not in the evening hours that is still an obligation or is that done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding from the investigation is that by the evening of 15 July 1995, those prisoners who were held in the school at Rocevic had -- the executions were being completed at Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if this is interpreted to mean the obligations to guard the remaining prisoners and the restoration of the terrain meaning to bury the dead prisoners, do we see Vinko Pandurevic's men involved in the actual executions which appears to be left out in this -- in this statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is left out in this statement, but the investigation through the years has identified soldiers from various battalions and subunits of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade involved in the actual executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have described fighting going on in this area on the 15th and -- most of it, you said, was the early morning hours of the 16th. How do you know that -- or that this restoration of this terrain, this burying of the bodies, is not a reference to cleaning up any battlefield dead on the day of the 14th or 15th in this area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, this comes back to why one of my analytical interests in the column, where it was located and what its activities were, throughout the course of the three days of the crimes, was so that I could verify that the military activities that we were seeing with respect to the engineer records related to burial operations, was not connected to casualties from the column but was, in fact, directly connected to the burial of bodies that were killed in the executions. The engineer company logbook, for example, of the Zvornik Brigade, reflects that the engineers are operating the bulldozers and bucket loaders are operating at locations on the 15th at Orahovac and at Petkovci. The column was not at those two locations, was kilometres away. Correspondingly, the work that they were doing was with the results of the human remains from the executions. It was not as a result of collecting human remains from the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And militarily, if this is -- situation is as urgent as described, being from the Muslim column from the rear, from the 2nd Corps of the front, would a military commander in your view be spending valuable resources going out into the woods to pick up dead?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I've testified with respect to this, I might understand Colonel Pandurevic expending and risking his soldiers' lives to recover the bodies of dead Serbian soldiers. He would not be doing the same to recover the bodies of dead Muslim soldiers in an area where there are still active combat operations occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by the evening of the 15th, were there any significant numbers of killed or battlefield wounded Serbian soldiers -- Bosnian Serb soldiers in those woods?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of casualties taken by the Army of the Republika Srpska in the Zvornik Brigade during the course of the war, the answer is yes. Perhaps 15 to 20 individuals who were either killed or wounded. Certainly the Army of the Republika Srpska and the Zvornik Brigade was not -- did not have casualties and dead bodies that would number hundreds and certainly would not account for the numbers that are found in those mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But my question was, Mr. Butler, would that have -- could that reference to burying bodies be such a significant resource drain that he would have been mentioning that to his corps command, burying any -- any of his own men at that point? I mean were his own men dead in the woods at that point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see your question, sorry, yes. It would not. I mean, he was talking clearly about burying other bodies. He was not burdening the corps command, telling his commander how difficult it is to bury dead Serbian soldiers who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And had there been any significant numbers killed based on your review at that time on the evening of 15 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Then we go on in the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you asked the question, had there been any significant numbers killed, killed among -- because we are talking about Serb soldiers being killed, and others being killed, what was your question about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll try to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your investigation indicate any Bosnian Serb soldiers that were in the defence of the Zvornik area dealing with the column and the 2nd Corps, were there any indications that any of them were killed on the early evening hours of 15 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as a component of his either interim report or the daily combat report, he talks about some casualties from the Zvornik Brigade, but that they only number at that time, I think, maybe four or five. They were firing from prepared positions in various locations, so at that juncture, he had not suffered the most serious casualties the brigade would suffer the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So to be absolutely clear, those roughly four or five, gathering them from their locations of wounding or death, would that be the kind of resource that he would be complaining to his forward command for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness answered that question already. That it was not. Were these four or five included in the 15 to 20 you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. If you look at the interim combat report and if you look at the third paragraph, I think it's perhaps the fourth or fifth line down, Colonel Pandurevic is explaining to the higher headquarters what he believes his casualties are at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't see it. Can you read what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line is: "So far, according to information received, we have four dead and a dozen or so wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's -- you earlier referred to 15 to 20 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Total. Yes, that's understood. That's clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then he goes on and says: "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer and it has neither the material nor other resources. If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." So tell us what you believe each of these sentences mean: "The command cannot take care of these problems any longer as it has neither the material nor the resources." He's listed quite a few problems above that. Which ones do you think he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context he's talking about both sets of problems. Obviously he is having to deal with the issues of the column. He's also cognizant of the personnel and material resources that the issue of dealing with the prisoners is having an impact. I mean, the reality is that the personnel, be they individuals who are guarding the prisoners, individuals who are involved in the execution, and individuals who are involved in the burial operations, I mean, these are all soldiers. And had it not been for the obligations of guarding the prisoners, and what follows subsequently, it stands to reason that these soldiers would be immediately put into the front lines and engaged in combat activity against the column, which, again, by Colonel Pandurevic's estimate of the size, is numerically superior to the forces that he's able to at that point on the battlefield array against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This last line here, "if no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go," who do you believe the "them" is in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified in the past, and it is still my belief, that in this particular sentence he's referring to the prisoners. Again, as a matter of fairness I understand that Colonel Pandurevic has a different interpretation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, why do you think he's referring to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, again, as it's been noted, as a course of the investigation, on the afternoon of 15 July, one of the first things that Colonel Pandurevic did was he had a meeting with his key staff officers as well as some of the police commanders at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, when he returned from Zepa, in order to fully acquaint himself with the situation. A number of the MUP individuals, as some of the documents note, their idea was that the Zvornik Brigade should let the column pass through so that they would minimise any risk to their own forces. Colonel Pandurevic obviously as the brigade commander denied that and in fact indicated that he intended to engage in battle against the column with the intention of destroying it in as much detail as he possibly could. It would be, in my mind, particularly this early on 15 July 1995, that the military situation, while it was deteriorating, it did not deteriorate to a state where this early Colonel Pandurevic was already considering letting the column go. He wanted, at this point in time, again looking at the totality of information that I'm aware of, he wanted to defeat the column. He understood the military capacity and threat that it represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I seek clarification perhaps from the parties rather than from the witness. The witness explains that he thinks the word "them" refers to the prisoners. Now, apparently, you also indicated that Mr. Pandurevic has a different interpretation of the word "them." I think for our minds it would be better listening to the evidence to know what the other interpretation is. Now, I do not know whether it's an interpretation which will be adopted by the Defence or not, or whether the parties agree on what the interpretation of the word "them" by Mr. Pandurevic is so that we are better able to listen focused to what seems to be in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was going to go there with another interpretation. And whether it's precisely Pandurevic's during his testimony, I don't recall, but there is one other clear interpretation that's been used in the Defence cases over the years and I was going to ask Mr. Butler about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, of course, usually a witness would not explain what a party's position in another case would be if the -- therefore I'm asking whether the parties agree on -- you understand, if we hear the evidence, if we know what the other possible interpretation is, you are better able to already start analysing the answer when you know what the competing interpretation of the word "them" would be. Therefore I'm also addressing the Defence whether they have a view on that or whether they could tell us anything about what in their view "them" would be. If not, we will continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this stage I think not. I think also that the relevant portion on the B/C/S original is not on the screen so I can't even view it, and since it's handwritten it would take me a while to even look at the context in which it's written. And as we sit here now, I personally don't know Pandurevic's view or explanation for this particular document. As you can imagine, the other trials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple answer therefore is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Butler doesn't need to comment on that, Mr. President, and I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I know that, but I was just asking whether we could create a situation in which the Chamber could, when listening and analysing the evidence of the witness, which you do at the moment you hear it, whether the competing interpretation of "them" was known. Apparently it's not. There is no agreement between the parties on what it is. Let's then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And that was my plan and my approach and we are almost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can I -- before we get there, Mr. Butler, you've mentioned that you believe based on the documents that Pandurevic wanted to destroy this Muslim group which we know are the remaining men from Srebrenica. Would he have done that -- would those have been his orders generated by himself or would those have come from higher command in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, he would be obviously following, if not the specific orders, certainly following the commander's intent, his leadership's intent that the column be militarily destroyed. It's not in isolation his order to do that. I mean, he's following within the context of the larger plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we now know, on the 16th, a corridor was opened up and after the fighting people were allowed to go through. Did you have any indication about how General Mladic felt about allowing these remnants of Srebrenica to walk through this open corridor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Indirectly, when Colonel Pandurevic opens the corridor on his own authority, this is not something he has previously coordinated with any of his superiors. As a result, what happens is that there is a flurry of communications between various channels of not only the army and of the civilian side to get clarification of what has happened. What ended up happening in context was that the state security organs of the Republika Srpska learned that the column was allowed to pass, they had informed the political leadership of the RS, the RS political leadership was inquiring of the army what was happening and if this, in fact, was the case. And again there is a series of intercepts where the military leadership is directing people who were in the Zvornik Brigade area to personally go find Colonel Pandurevic and get an explanation for what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll see that document a little later if we have time. Now, getting back to this document in front of us, "if no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go," what is your understanding of Pandurevic's Defence version of this? Or his -- what does Pandurevic say about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my recollection of Colonel Pandurevic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we have -- if counsel has the testimony of Pandurevic that we could be put in e-court and on the screen, that's one thing, but they have a witness referring to testimony from another case that's not before us, that we don't have a means of immediately verifying and I don't think that's proper even for an expert witness. I mean, I think that the -- if it's something that's not referenced in evidence or in a report, we are entitled to see it and then have the -- the witness can comment upon it and give his opinions upon it, but to have a witness, even an expert witness, try to recollect what another party's evidence in another proceeding was, I think is just -- it's open to error, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'm okay with that. We can get to where I know the Trial Chamber wants to go without referencing Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That at least would then meet the concerns of Mr. Ivetic. Now, if you can do it in another way, then please do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, there has been an interpretation of this by others and I don't want to put any value judgement on it, that you have been made aware of in cross-examination over the years. Can you tell us what that interpretation is and what you think of it? For example, what does that interpretation say that "I will be forced to let them go," what is the reference -- what is that reference according to this other interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that's the exact same question even in a worse light because now we have an unknown source which we therefore then can't [indiscernible] and verify it. For an expert that's precisely what they are not supposed to do according to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll put a few questions to the witness. Mr. Butler, were you ever -- did you ever receive any information about what Mr. Pandurevic's position on the interpretation of this line would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom did you receive that or how did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even though I was not here, I did follow the transcripts of Colonel Pandurevic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you learned that from reading the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The public transcripts of his testimony, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you tell us what was your understanding of the position of Pandurevic as based on the reading of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again, if I recall the transcripts correctly, his interpretation was that he was referring to -- letting them go being letting the column go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you read that in view of the -- your own research, did you consider this to be consistent with your research, and if not, where did you find the inconsistency, what led you to believe that that could not be the proper answer to such a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think I -- I hope I alluded to it in some of my prior testimony maybe 10 or 15 minutes ago. It is not consistent with my belief of what the interpretation of this line is, with respect to letting them go, and it is not because of my understanding of the context of the meeting that took place at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on the arrival of Colonel Pandurevic and Colonel Pandurevic's stated intention of militarily engaging the column with the intention of defeating it to the detail he believed he could do. And then suddenly, several hours later, without a significant change in circumstances, Colonel Pandurevic is essentially, if one reads this the way that it takes it as, under Colonel Pandurevic's view, he's essentially threatening the corps commander that: If you don't send additional resources, I will in essence abdicate my military responsibilities of attacking the column as a soldier and I will let them escape. So again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Them" now being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Them" being the column. Again, taking Colonel Pandurevic's view as a result of his testimony on this. So again, I accept obviously that this is Colonel Pandurevic's position and why it is his position. I don't think it is logically supported by the prevailing events that are happening on the ground at the time. But again, as I said earlier, I do understand there are two schools of thought on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And yours is let them -- "I'll let them go" is let the prisoners go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you consider in this analysis that this term, "I will be forced to let them go," is immediately below the -- or not immediately below but right -- right below what you have described as the guarding and burying of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if Pandurevic is -- under your interpretation is -- appears to be obviously frustrated or concerned about all these prisoners in his zone, do we see him indicate any similar frustration to those very same prisoners in any other documents, shortly after this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, on 18 July 1995, again, Colonel Pandurevic will author an interim combat report to the command of the Drina Corps, essentially laying out his case for what actions he took and why he took them and why he believed he was justified in doing so. One of the things that he raises, as he says in his interim combat report, is the issue that somebody made the decision to put all of these prisoners in schools in his municipality, and I think we will get to that document and the exact wording of that is evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will try to get to that document. Let's go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question still about this document? The next line reads: "I made an offer to the commander of the other side to separate out the civilian and have the others surrender." Is there any documentary support for that elsewhere, that they apparently would have negotiated to distinguish between military and civilians and then at least let the civilians go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your question, sir. I know that there are intercept communications and there may even be in some of the combat reports discussions where Colonel Pandurevic or other individuals from the Zvornik Brigade are aware that the Bosnian Muslim forces in the column have been talking with their corresponding Bosnian Serb military counterparts, and that there have been various offers going back and forth. The Bosnian Muslims obviously wished to go out as a complete column, and the Bosnian Serb position has been, We would be willing to let potentially the civilians go but all of the military personnel must surrender, in essence be taken prisoner by them. So under the circumstances neither side, particularly on the 15th of July, felt that they would accept those -- those terms with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is there any documentary evidence of meetings or communications between the parties, apart from internal discussions within one party about what to do or what not to do, is there any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any face-to-face discussions. These negotiations took place over radio networks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Radio networks between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean they used common equipment. They knew what frequencies each was on, and so I believe that Dusko Vukotic, the intelligence officer from the Zvornik Brigade, was the actual radio telephonic go-between because of where he was located between -- that would relay offers by the Bosnian Muslim side to the Bosnian Serb side and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did those communications which are described now here in the interim combat report, did they continue after this report was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they continued all the way through the ultimate decision by Colonel Pandurevic to let the column go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, in that regard, are you aware of the tactical intercepts that were taken by the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall if a person name Semso Muminovic was involved in this negotiation in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was the principal party on the Muslim side seeking to make this -- to negotiate the release of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, P1501. And this is the duty officer notebook of the Zvornik Brigade, the teacher's edition so we should go to page 79 in the English and page 78 in the B/C/S, and we are now into 16 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I'm drawing your attention to the centre of the page, and the Trial Chamber has heard about what this book is and how these notes are done, but can you tell us, this reference, 0855, Golic asked Popovic to call him and said that he can forget what he asked for and what he wrote about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you stop for a moment? We need it back on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. "He knows what he's supposed to do, according to the agreed procedure (boss from Panorama 01) message conveyed to Popovic at 0910." Okay, tell us, Golic, as everyone knows is, a relatively common name. Can you tell us who you believe in the context of this Golic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
