utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is Major Golic, one of the security officers at the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it -- we talked about Golic in the last day or two with documents. Was he a security officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he is a -- he is an intelligence officer in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Popovic, this Popovic, who do you believe it is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic who is the chief of security for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And has your investigation revealed what it was that -- that Popovic is asking for, what this reference was that he can forget about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've ever been able to put that in a context, that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And here on the 16th of July, what, very briefly, has your analysis shown that Popovic is up to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the 16th of July, there is a number of intercepts as well as documents which reflect that Colonel Popovic is in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and that he is engaged in seeking to get fuel to the village of Pilica. When one looks in this in context of the larger issues that are occurring, and again there is documents and material related to it in intercepts, Colonel Pandurevic -- Colonel Popovic is involved with the execution of the prisoners up at Pilica and in the Dom of Culture, who are ultimately killed in either Branjevo or in the Dom of Culture, and that at some juncture they run out of fuel in order to transport prisoners from Pilica to the dome. So there is a large body of information that reflects his activity dealing with the Zvornik Brigade and the Drina Corps to ensure that fuel can be sent to Pilica, as he says in his own words in the intercept, to complete the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. As we go through this it then says: "He knows what he's supposed to do, according to the agreed procedure, boss from Panorama 01." Now, who would the boss from Panorama 01 be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Panorama is the telephonic code name for the Main Staff headquarters. As part of the military vernacular that they used, when you see the suffix 01 after that, you are to take that as being the commander personally. There will be notations of Panorama 01, the commander personally being General Mladic. Zlatar 01, the commander, depending on which day it is, either General Zivanovic or General Krstic. Same with Zvornik, Palma 01 being Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I just confirm that the B/C/S original says: "Glavni sa Panorama 1," it does not say "boss."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first look at the original. I don't know whether it can be enlarged. Can it be -- could you, looking at the original, Mr. Ivetic, take us to what line of this 855 entry? Please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is the second-to-last line of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are looking at the portion between the brackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slowly read that, and again it's not a verification of the translation but to see whether there may be a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would begin now in B/C/S: "Glavni sa Panorama 01."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was not translated to us at this moment -- interpreted. I should make the distinction. Glavni would stand for, and I'm seeking the assistance of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'm sorry, they may have rules about the official CLSS, I don't know, but if your question could include the whole sentence so that we can get it in context? Words by themselves may mean different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the only thing is that the parts within brackets seems to be in dispute. Again, not to give the final word but if I would pronounce these words, as -- and if I would be able to do it exactly the same way as Mr. Ivetic did, how would that be interpreted for us at this moment? Could the booth tell us. And, again, if there is any possible inconsistency with the translation as we find it on paper, it will be formally submitted to CLSS for verification of the translation, but if there is no need at all to do it, we would avoid it. Could I hear from the English booth? I don't hear anything. I never know whether to look to the right or to the left but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we were on the wrong channel. Could Mr. Ivetic please repeat once again the exact words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just the four words, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And now I switch to B/C/S. [Interpretation] The main one from Panorama 01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The main one" instead of "the boss." I think whether -- Mr. McCloskey's body language tells me that he considers the main one to be the same as the boss. It will be submitted, this specific line, for verification to CLSS. May I take it that you'll take the initiative Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to reiterate, Mr. Butler, you're talking about the words "Panorama 01." What does that refer to, if we forget about the boss or the main one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he has explained that. He has compared Panorama 01 to Zlatar 01, et cetera, and then it will always be the -- the person at the top of that unit or organisation. I think we heard that a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Pages 46, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted him to do it -- make sure it's the same if it was separate from this what may be a confusing reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And message conveyed to Popovic at 910, that's -- that speaks for itself. We will talk about that a bit later, so let's go to the next intercept, 1329. And has your analysis over the years determined that this intercept was on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us who you believe Cerovic is in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cerovic in this context is Colonel Cerovic who is the assistant commander for morale and legal affairs for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't go through it all but we hear that there is this -- Cerovic is telling Beara that triage needs to be done. And what do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As the investigation has laid out, the prisoners that were being held in the schools from the 14th through the 16th of July, 1995, did not receive any medical treatment whatsoever. In this context, and given the fact that the orders go to Colonel Beara in that particular sense, he's obviously not a medical doctor, I take this to refer to a euphemism that the remaining prisoners are to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if Cerovic is at the Drina Corps command at Vlasenica and we go down and see that he says: "Trkulja was here with me just now and he was looking for you," meaning I take it Beara, "I don't know." And Beara says: "Yes." And Cerovic says: "So he told me he got instructions from above." Remind us who Trkulja is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Trkulja is an officer on the Main Staff, his staff responsibility includes oversight of armour and mechanised forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if he got this information about triage from above, who do you -- who would you take that to include?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular context, being he is an officer, a senior officer of the Main Staff, above would be those officers appointed over him, General Major Miletic and General Major -- Lieutenant General Krstic -- I'm sorry, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see that Beara says: "I don't want to talk about it on the phone." Would that be -- would that support your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Clearly this is a topic, going back to knowing that their communications were susceptible to being intercepted, it was not something that they wanted out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But first I would like to look at the transcript. On page 47, line 1, it seems as if I rose and confirmed what the B/C/S original said, but it was Mr. Ivetic who did so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are going back, P1501, page 81 in the English, page 80 in the B/C/S. Back to the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook. We are still on 16 July. And to remind us that that intercept we just saw was noted to be at 1111 hours. And we see a note here in the duty officer notebook: "At 1115 hours it was reported from Zlatar that a triage of wounded and prisoners must be carried out," and then in parentheses, "it was reported to Beara." And do you connect this in any way with the intercept we saw that happened just a few minutes earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1333. And again, do you know from your study that this intercept was on 16 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you can probably see the hard copy, we haven't got there quite yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if -- for the Serbian version, if we can take a minute to let folks read that and then flip it to the rest of it where the body, I think, of the intercept is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had made a brief reference earlier about Popovic and Pilica and things. Looking at this intercept between Zlatar and Palma, so between the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade, we see the Palma duty officer talking -- saying that 500 litres of diesel fuel for Lieutenant Popovic. And then we see them - just go down - speaking of a bit more and then Basovic gets on the line. Who do you believe Basovic to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Basovic is a technical services officer with the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we go down a little bit further it says: "Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is here at Palma, you know," we know what that means, and Popovic is at Palma, and then -- and then P, the Palma duty officer says: "500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for or else the work he's doing will stop." And then it goes on and actually mentions that a bus loaded with oil is to go to the Pilica village. What work do you believe this is referring to, and what work do you know was going on in the Pilica area on the 16th of July at about 1358 hours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my understanding from the investigation is that at that time, buses were still bringing prisoners from the school in Kula and Pilica to Branjevo where they were being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page in English. And we see here that there are references to Golic and Pop and the 500 litres. Who do you believe Pop is in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pop is a nickname for Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then finally there is a reference about -- to Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. Remind us of his position and how he may fit into this, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic is someone we've heard earlier on the intercepts. He is the chief of transportation services for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you aware, we have just seen this reference to Popovic and the procedure from Panorama 01 and now we see this reference to fuel and Pilica, were you aware in your study that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was involved in any legitimate counter-intelligence or military-legal work on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go now again back to the duty officer notebook. But it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. McCloskey. But could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Can we go to P1501, page 85 in the English, page 84 in the Serbian, it's the duty officer notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we had just left this intercept from 1358 hours about Popovic and fuel to Pilica. And now we are on a page that we have identified as 16 July. There we go. And we see this notation now this -- this intercept was 1358, this notation at 1400 hours, Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2. Do you connect this to the intercept we just saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it notes that Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed. And also at the bottom of this, there is a notation, that they called from Zlatar, that the commander is to call the Zlatar duty officer or send a report on the situation in the field. So we know that the call from the Drina Corps and the commander. Who do you take the commander to be? Who does -- what -- who is Drina Corps looking for here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, in the context of who is taking the call, the commander that they are referring to is Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Drina Corps duty officer wants him to send a written report on the situation in the field at 1525. Again, tell us briefly what this is about. How it fits into what you've been saying, but very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again in context of what's happening on the ground, this is about the time that word starts to get out that Colonel Pandurevic has concluded a temporary battlefield truce with the column and is allowing the column to depart Republika Srpska territory and enter ABiH-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to the next document now. It's 65 ter 4271. And this is a logistics document that we picked up from the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how, if at all, can you relate this to this intercept and the note -- the notebook reference to Popovic and fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it's related. Clearly it is a routine fuel receipt reflecting that on a certain day and time, so many litres, 500 litres exactly, were allotted to Popovic, Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is noted in block 15 and 140 litres were returned. In a broader sense, this document takes us back to a discussion that we had at the beginning of my testimony about analysis related to authenticating the body of intercepts. Here you have a routine fuel document receipt that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997, buried in one of dozens of binders in the technical services office of the Zvornik Brigade, that exactly corresponds to an intercepted communication that the ABiH had in July of 1995 and obviously neither party had any awareness of the other's holding of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also briefly, what does it tell us, if anything, about a security officer's ability to obtain resources on his own or outside the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As briefly as I can, obviously under the circumstances, one of the primary defences of many of the commanders in previous proceedings has been that the security officers essentially and unlawfully took control of various military units in order to have their way conducting these mass executions and that the commanders and their other representatives had no knowledge or were otherwise in no way involved. This particular vignette where you're looking at a security officer of the Drina Corps, obviously a powerful person, still having to follow the normal military channels to obtain fuel, the normal military bureaucracy, even though it's for a crime, and he's being disbursed the fuel and he's having to turn in the remainder of the fuel, is -- in my opinion supports the fact that the chain of command and the military bureaucracy associated with it was functioning normally even though it was engaged in the commission of a large-scale criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the same topic, again briefly, taking us back just in our memories to the conversation between Beara and Zivanovic and Beara and Krstic, where Beara is trying to get resources of men to do his -- to carry out the executions, how does the fact that you have a -- the Colonel from the Main Staff going to a Drina Corps general fit into this analysis about the power and any potential independence of even a Main Staff security officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Beara clearly, as a Main Staff security officer, had a wide-ranging set of powers. Having said that, those powers and authorities did not include the ability to essentially order troops that were not subordinate to him to commit any act, whether it was a legitimate military act or a crime. He had to talk to the commanders of those units, Colonel or General Zivanovic first when he thought he was the commander, and then when learning he was no longer the commander, General Krstic, in order to seek his authorisation to make those troops available. So again, it goes back to my view that the military security officials, while committing very unfortunate and in fact criminal acts, they were heavily involved in that, they were doing that within the wider context of their normal military authorities. They could not have done these acts unless their commanders had directed them to do that and, again, it's been an issue in various courts through the years going back and forth on this particular issue. It is my opinion that, again, this and other documents of this sort lay the foundation and confirms my view that the military chain of command was functioning as it was supposed to function under the JNA rules and regulations that were in effect, that the officers were ordering the acts within the competence of their authorities, and that the security branch did not mutiny somehow or otherwise unlawfully usurp the powers that were granted to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04271 receives number P2127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: P1501, please, page 87 in the English, page 86 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So back to the duty officer notebook for 16 July, and you just testified that you were not aware of any counter-intelligence or military-legal jobs that Popovic was doing or something to that effect. But on this page, we can see in the middle of -- just below the middle of the page, that the Zvornik Brigade gets a message from Zlatar that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic must go to Vinko Pandurevic in the field at 1640 hours and this is the message through the 1st Battalion that Popovic must report to the duty officer so he can be sent on to the task by Zlatar. So first of all, why do you think this is the message has to go through the 1st Battalion and where is that in relation to these events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone or the area of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade encompasses the village of Pilica and the area around Branjevo, the school at Kula, so the fact that they had to reach Popovic through the 1st Battalion corresponds to the fact that he was in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you believe the subject matter of this message is about? Why is it that the Drina Corps command is now telling Popovic he's got to go see Pandurevic in the field? And of course tell us where you think Pandurevic is on the afternoon of the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that at this point in time Colonel Pandurevic is at his forward command post. At this point in time, as the investigation notes, the decision has been made by Colonel Pandurevic to allow the column to leave VRS territory. Word of that decision is being heard in various locations by various officials, but at that point in time, no one is able to confirm this is accurate information because nobody has heard anything from Colonel Pandurevic. So Zlatar, the Drina Corps headquarters, and the duty officer there, knowing that they have a Drina Corps officer in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, is seeking to get him out to talk to Colonel Pandurevic so somebody can report back to the Drina Corps what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to an intercept P1338. And this is an intercept from the 16th of July, a CSB intercept, at 1615 hours, so close to the time from that last page, where a conversation was recorded between the Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic, who was not audible. So it's important in looking at this to understand that we are only hearing one side of the conversation in this. Is that correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we are just hearing what the Main Staff duty officer is saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just a bit of it I'll get out. "Well, it's like this, I've just sent a telegram to Toso." I think you've told us Toso you believe to be a nickname for Tolimir. And where is Tolimir on the 16th, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's engaged in dealing with military operations around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says: "Well, the president called a short while ago, and he said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic had arranged passage for the Muslims over that territory." The president, who do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president would be President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Karisik who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, if I'm correct in remembering, he is head of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska State Security Service, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then the Main Staff person says, we can read for ourselves about what he's saying about communication and that he's waiting, waiting for them to call because Pandurevic hasn't called for the last hour so we see that Pandurevic is a bit out of touch. And then there is this note about both fighters and civilians. Then he says: "I spoke to Krsto down there, he's saying that it's going well but he didn't say how far they got but he says it's going well." What, in your view, if we have the Main Staff duty officer telling this to General Mladic, who do you believe he means when he's saying Krsto?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again in this context, it would be General Krstic, the commander of the Drina Corps, and who now is also obviously engaged in military operations against the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when he says he didn't know how far they got, what's he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again they are advancing towards Zepa and again the reflection that he doesn't know how far down a particular axis of advance or what it -- how far his troops had gotten at a certain point of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there is a comment: "According to Maric, yes, it's solved." Is there a Maric you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again I believe there is a General Maric who is the chief of air and air defence forces for the VRS at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what was solved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then it talks about captured equipment at four UN check-points down in Zepa. And has there been information about that independent of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From what -- roughly, what source of documents did you read that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is a notation of this in documents related to the -- from the Drina Corps talking about the -- either the Rogatica Brigade or the Drina Corps talking about the capture of these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we see: "Good, there were no other major problems. Up on Majevica there was something but that's been solved." Majevica, do you know where that is, whose -- what corps's zone that's in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's East Bosnia Corps, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so what do you take this -- these comments of the duty officer to General Mladic to be? Just ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of what is happening with the column, nor -- as it would be a normal military practice, the duty officer is briefing the commander on the events on the ground and noting the fact that at that point in time, here is their understanding of the situation and further noting that nobody has heard anything from Colonel Pandurevic directly yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if General Mladic was in Belgrade receiving this information and saying whatever he said, would that, in your view, be an exercise of command by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As a commander, whether he's physically on the ground or not in a certain location, he's going to want to be kept fully abreast of the relevant military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1513. It's a -- from the command of the Zvornik Brigade, 16 July now, another interim combat report from Vinko Pandurevic that we can see if we look at the Serbian version. And this is now, we can see, talking about the battle I think that you've mentioned on the 16th, he refers to it as a synchronised kamikaze attack on the 4th Battalion position. Using their numerical advantage they surrounded the 4th Battalion. Counting soldiers and civilians, armed and unarmed, altogether 7.000. 7.000, can you make anything of that number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is Colonel Pandurevic's assessment of the column. I again -- the actual -- I've never done specific research with respect to the total number of people who came out from the column on the other side. As I've explained earlier, it wasn't pertinent to why I needed to research the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then it goes on to note that there were examples of jumping on tanks and self-propelled guns, that by throwing themselves they captured three 76 millimetre self-propelled guns and seized trenches, and basically overran those positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it goes on under paragraph 2 to say: "We sustained dozens of wounded, about ten dead and five missing." We can see also the rest of that with supplies and evacuating wounded. And then in paragraph 3 he says: "In view of the great pressure on the brigade's area of responsibility, the losses sustained, the inability of the surrounded forces to hold out for long, the abandonment of the Zvornik PBR command to deal as best it could with the Srebrenica Turks and served it right when it was the brigade that forced them out of Srebrenica into its own area." What do you take that to mean, just briefly, that comment he's saying that it served them right? I think he's speaking about his own forces, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Pandurevic and two battle groups from the Zvornik Brigade did in fact participate in the operations to eliminate the Srebrenica safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Coupled with an absolute determination of the Turks to save some -- to save at least some lives," it goes on, "in order to prevent losses in our own ranks, I have decided in view of the situation to open a corridor along the line of the three lost trenches for the civilian population, about 7.000 of them ..." So he's now saying of the 7 -- about 5.000 of them, excuse me. So he's saying of the 7.000, 5.000 of them are civilians. "I have agreed on a method of evacuation with the enemy and this is now going forward. I have requested the release of captured policemen on my own missing soldiers -- and my own missing soldiers." So is this the reference to the opening of the corridor that you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any indication that Pandurevic received an order to do that or even authorisation from his superiors to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. He goes on on the next page in English: "This procedure is in progress and I think it will succeed. It is likely that a certain number of soldiers got out among the civilians but all who passed, passed through unarmed." What do you make of that comment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that comment is actually a tad self-serving, by Colonel Pandurevic, in order to protect himself from criticism. Clearly, those soldiers who were able to break through did so with their weapons. They were not disarmed by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, and this is an intercept that we will try to get through this, P1350. And you can see, Mr. Butler, from your hard copy, this is a 2116 hours intercept, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, Rasic, Popovic has asked to be connected to General Krstic at Zlatar. Is this an intercept that you know to be from the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just want to take you down to the middle of the page, we can see that -- that he, Popovic says that: "I was with the boss personally." Who do you think he's referring to here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pandurevic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Is that connected to what you've talked to about before, Popovic being sent over there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then he mentions: "Well, you got his interim report," and was that the report we just looked at, P1513?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Popovic says: "It's all just like he wrote, I was there on the spot, and saw for myself he had received some numbers. Well, that's not even important. I'll come there tomorrow so tell the general I've finished the job." What in your view is he talking about here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've testified to this line before and, again, with the exception of the last phrase, Colonel Popovic is talking about the situation with respect to his discussion with Colonel Pandurevic. His last phrase "I finished the job," it is my view that in that context, Colonel Popovic is informing the people at the Drina Corps headquarters that he's finished his particular job which would be, at that point in time, completed the execution of the prisoners up in the Pilica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in the first part of that he's saying, "it's just like he wrote, he had received some numbers," which numbers do you think he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it at this juncture that he's talking about the numbers with respect to the size of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Rasic goes on to confirm: "You finished." Popovic: "I finished everything." "Good." Popovic says: "I'll come there tomorrow when I'm sure that it's all been taken care of, you know." Rasic: "Good." "After I bring a transport from here." "Right." Then Popovic says: "Well, in general there weren't any major problems. But up there, there were horrible problems. And that thing the commander sent, it was just right." When he says "up there, there were horrible problems," what do you think he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is referring in this particular context, "up there" meaning the area close to Baljkovica, since it's actually a geographical rise from Zvornik, being in the valley, towards Baljkovica, which is being up the valley. So he's using this as a reference, "up there" meaning where the battle was being fought at Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now, let's -- so then he goes on to say, Popovic says: "Just the thing. Horrible, it was horrible." What's that a reference to, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I've testified before, and I still believe it to be the case that in this juncture he's talking about his role in the executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's look at the next page, page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, it also reads: "That thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing." What do you understand to be the thing that was sent which was the right thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Earlier that day, the Drina Corps made arrangements to send another company-sized unit that they had cobbled together from the Bratunac area to reinforce the forces in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then let's go to page 2, and Mr. Butler, can you briefly explain to us the -- was that your initial analysis of this intercept back in the Krstic days or have you changed it when we look at this? Let us finish it up when -- we see that the next question is: Did anything arrive from Vidoje Blagojevic? And that would be from where?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the Bratunac Brigade, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Popovic says: "You mean manpower." "Yes, yes." "Yes, it arrived but it didn't arrive on time, and it wasn't brought in on time and the others who arrived did arrive but they were late and so they weren't brought in on time and that's why the commander who was there had problems." And then it says: "When exactly did Blagojevic's men arrived?" "Fuck it, I don't know exactly." "I know." And then they go down. The question is asked again about Blagojevic's men, and someone, the -- D says he'll call right back about that. What was your -- I mean the Court has heard evidence that men from Bratunac, is the way it's described, arrived at the Pilica farm after the 10th Sabotage had already been working. What was your first analysis of this and did you change it and why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My initial analysis of this intercept in the Krstic case reflected that I believed that when they talked about the issue with respect to first the men coming up, the boss sent them and it was right for the job, we did have knowledge of the fact that men from Bratunac were sent to Pilica and did participate in the executions of at least some of the people at Branjevo, and I testified to that in the Krstic case. Subsequently, as the investigation is continued, obviously, through time, new information came to my attention in the form of other documents as well as explanations from VRS officers that we were able to interview, and they explained that, no, in particular, these people were soldiers from another unit, the Bratunac Brigade, and they were sent for military purpose. Again, when I make my analysis of this broader body of information and I've done over the years, my analysis is based on the documents and the context as I understand it at the time. I'm not locked into any position for any reason. If I receive new information that would challenge one of my earlier conclusions or reflect the fact that I painted the context erroneously and that there is another interpretation of it, if it's correct I will adopt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's -- we are still on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go very briefly to P1147, it's V0009267.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a video you have seen so I just want to remind us briefly of a few seconds of it. And if I've got it right, it should be Mladic at the VMA on the 16th, in uniform, speaking on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that should be at 44 -- sorry, 49229.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for whatever reason we don't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No transcript has been provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please, interpreters, this is the -- this is the Srebrenica trial video and I believe we've decided we don't need over-translation with the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there would be any challenge to the subtitles. Okay. It will be played again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we can stop it there at 49572. And if we could now just go to the transcript of that, it's e-court page 94 in English and it should be e-court page 90 in the Serbian, which should be the transcript of the little blurb we saw. I think we were able to read the subtitles about the reference to Legenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what I wanted to ask you about, Mr. Butler, starts where when Mladic, as we note, in the English, speaking into the telephone: "Well, then you should send Gojko, have him come over tonight and send two more cars." In your time, did you know the name of Mladic's driver?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have in English what we see in B/C/S? I don't think so. It looks like a transcript of one of the Hotel Fontana meetings, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the right page in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be e-court page 90. I'm sorry, it's 94 in English and 90 in the B/C/S, thank you, which I had stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have the correct pages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see where it starts with Mladic speaking on the telephone. Did you, in your time, ever learn the name of one of Mladic's drivers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my time here with the Tribunal, no, but I do understand that the investigation has identified one of his drivers as an individual named Gojko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "Have him come over tonight and sent two more cars, two more cars, and have him report here tonight. I am not going while they are in the air." Do you have an opinion on what that could mean? Or does mean? This reference to "I am not going while they are in the air"? Do we know of anybody in the air on this -- this would be the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in fact, NATO military aircraft are active over the Zepa enclave on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then as it goes down he makes a reference: "Okay, here is what we'll do. How about at the stadium at Legenda's place." Now, Legenda, is that Milan Jolovic of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it says: "Great. You don't have to send a car for me, I'll get there. Here you send two cars, have them report to tomorrow." And then it says who to report to and talks about Milan Lesic, which I'm sure the Defence will agree is one of the Canadian Serbs that was there at the VMA. All right. And then he says, down farther: "Fine, let him do it, no need, there is no need. He has to bear in mind, just send him a telegram that I will see them there, right, so they don't hit me, let them pound the NATO." What do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a cryptic thing but understanding that the RS may -- the air-on-air defence forces may engage NATO aircraft, he certainly doesn't want to get targeted inadvertently by his own air defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this line, "and what about from Vinko's," who do you take Vinko to be in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then he says: "Very well, full steam ahead, maximum security, and don't wait for the orders. As soon as they show up in the air, shoot them down. You don't care if they are Turkish or others. Is it possible they are from the Turkey, comment, they were hitting from high altitude, whatever, shoot them down at high altitude, doesn't matter where they crash as long as they crash. All right, bro, cheers, we will be in touch." And then Mladic states: "NATO struck, NATO struck."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I guess we need to -- thank you, we need to go to the next page in e-court for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "There are no killed or wounded there at Zepa, let's go." And did that assist in your evaluation that this could be referring to the NATO air over Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this and other military documents that reflect that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document. I have it as 65 ter 04126. And this is a regular combat report from the Drina Corps in the name of General Krstic. And just looking at the front page -- well, if we look at the rear page it's got a time stamp of 1937 and 2010 so if -- it's the evening as it should be. Just looking at that first page in English, down right about the last paragraph of the first -- of number 1, it says: "According to reports submitted by subordinate units, there are around 300 armed -- 3.000 armed soldiers and civilian in Pandurica, Planinci, Crni Vrh, Glodjansko Brdo sector." Is that the Zvornik Brigade sector?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it says: "NATO bombed the Zepa sector and according to initial reports there was no damage or casualties." Now, is this information consistent with what we just heard Mladic saying, first over the telephone to someone, and then to the group of people -- then another statement a group of people in front of him there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04126 receives number P2128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 21039C?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see this is at 2126 hours, which was just a few minutes after that 2116 hours conversation which was P1350, where they kept asking Popovic to find out when the other forces showed up. And so we can see here that there is a small note from the intercept operators. And do you know this to be the 16th of July as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Colonel Cerovic was informed that at 2100, 30 men came from Badem from Blagojevic. And then at 1705, 30 men came from Dobus [phoen] and 100 men came from Banja Luka. Was this one of the intercepts to help change your conclusion that the men from -- from Blagojevic could not have been the men that came to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this was one of the pieces of information as well as other information that came to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: According to this, they would have arrived at 1705 in the afternoon, and is that -- does that fit with the account of when the people from Bratunac showed up at Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I wanted to ask you about, mainly, here, is it -- it also has a short reference that General Mladic asked through Colonel Cerovic, and so that would have been through what -- where would Colonel Cerovic have been in your view here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time he would be at the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he asked what had happened to the three self-propelled guns, and at 2135 the duty officer informed him that the guns were on the Serbian side. These three self-propelled guns, do you connect them in any way with the three self-propelled guns that we saw Pandurevic say were taken from him on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what does that indicate to you about the kind of information General Mladic is getting regarding these events that are occurring on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As one might expect under the circumstances, he is keeping well informed of what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, that needs to be offered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Same objection to the intercepts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same objection. Any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. This is part of the collection we have a document with a P number that reflects this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same objection, same response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A simple way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assign a number for this intercept so that be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21039C receives number P2129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for your information, that same intercept is in evidence at P1352 but a different version, and all these versions need to be fit together and it's important to have them, in our view. But I leave it at that and go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it's hereby on the record that the two can be linked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. P1667, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are at 16 July still. This is a morning intercept, got a bit off our chronology. And it's between X and Y, and it says, in pertinent part for us, until 2030 -- Y says: "Until 2030." X says: "Yes." Y says: "All right." X says: "CER signal." Y says: "CER signal." Have you learned what CER signal means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you believe it means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, again from looking at various documents with respect to communication protocols, is that at this point in time the signal CER is to reflect a weapons-type posture with respect to air defence weapons, which means that they are not authorised to shoot at aerial targets for a certain time. And I believe there is a subsequent document where, in fact, in the duty officer logbook it actually identifies what CER is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to that again. P1501, page 91 in the English, page 90 in the Serbian. And we see here that the duty officer has written in the book at 2020 hours, the signal CER was sent from Zlatar. It says: "I.e., it's forbidden to shoot at aerial targets until 2200 hours, all units informed about that." And would that include a helicopter coming from Serbia landing at some site in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the broadest sense, you do these things to avoid a situation where your own air defence forces inadvertently launch an attack on friendly aircraft. So I mean that that you've mentioned, that scenario would qualify as to why you would want to have a signal in place so that friendly forces don't fire on friendly aircraft by accident, especially at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just below that, we see: Message from Zlatar that a parcel set off from Badem half an hour ago, and it was reported at 2015 hours. In this context, what do you take a parcel to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular context, I am not aware of additional prisoners being moved from Bratunac, so I take this to be additional soldiers or troops being moved up to the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document, P01579. And the Trial Chamber has seen this document but I'd like it if we could get your brief take on the two different parts of it. We see that it's a 17 July document in the name of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- Mr. President, we've asked that a revised translation be uploaded into e-court because this one did not have the SR on it, so -- which the original did, so our revised one has that and it's doc ID 05257985-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you want this to replace the translation which is present in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any, as usual, improved or corrected translations can be revisited by the other party within 48 hours, but at this time, has it been uploaded, Madam Registrar, so that you can replace it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm unable to locate the translation in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do the following. The original is with SR after the name of Mr. Mladic, whereas the translation is not. Therefore, we can work on it but it has to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We think it might be findable if you put a dash, 0525-79 -- sorry, 0425-7985. I probably misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, does that resolve the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With number 4, yes, it's there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the revised translation may replace the one which was in e-court until now. Madam Registrar, would you please do that. And let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this document that Mladic -- under Mladic's name, we see these first two paragraphs, he says to send these three officers from the Main Staff, the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, and to assist in joining the VRS and MUP forces in the planning and coordination of combat operations to block, crush and destroy lagging Muslim forces in the wider area of Kamenica and Cerska; number 2, the team from the VRS shall assess the situation on the brigade's front and in the rear, the available forces, and hear out the proposal and opinion of the commander of the 1st Zvornik Brigade and then they are to draw up a plan together, comb the terrain, crush and destroy the groups in the wider area of Kamenica. Just summarised briefly there. In your view and analysis and what you know, is this -- is this really what this is about or what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I am aware that the actual purpose of these officers going up to the Zvornik Brigade is to determine the circumstances surrounding why Colonel Pandurevic allowed the column to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And paragraph 3, we see a discussion or a -- the order talking about a 17 July and it lists various forces in this area that we are all familiar with now in the Bratunac area, to discover and destroy Muslim groups, and were there Muslim groups in that area on this date, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Mladic says: "I hereby appoint Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, the officer for the military police in the Main Staff security administration as the commander of all the aforementioned forces to conduct the aforementioned task." Now -- and then he's supposed to get back by the 19th of July with a proposal. Were you aware who was in command of those forces on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Colonel Blagojevic was in command of those forces on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, 1995, there is a Bratunac Brigade daily combat report where the duty officer reflects that Colonel Blagojevic was visiting those various units and directing their tasks. The day previous to that a Drina Corps officer, Colonel Milanovic, I believe is his name, had made those proposals that given the chaotic situation on the road and the fact that you had units from the military police, the civilian police and the Bratunac Brigade as well as the 5th Engineers engaged, that they should appoint one individual and he recommended the Bratunac Brigade commander to take control of all of the activities in order to ensure that the military actions against that part of the column were fully synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. On 17 July, do you know where Colonel Blagojevic was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He -- on the 17th, he received orders to lead additional troops from the Bratunac Brigade to Zepa in order to in part make up for the forces that Colonel Pandurevic had left with, so when he departed the brigade area with those forces or at the head of those forces, he was no longer available to take command of the operations there. It was because Colonel Blagojevic was leaving that the Main Staff felt that they had to appoint another officer in order to fulfil the task and ensure that the military operations were properly synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who, in your view, was the -- in command of those forces on 17 July after Blagojevic left?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it break time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the -- could Mr. Mladic keep his volume low. Waiting for the witness. I come back to the code names for Panorama and Palma and Badem and Zlatar. It's a nice example of how time is wasted. It is proposed as an adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence objected to it to be -- to be acknowledged of it being taken judicial notice of, although they do agree, apparently, they said it's notorious, and then we start hearing evidence on that. Both parties are not doing what they are supposed to do, that is to look at facts as facts and not at why the fact is presented for establishing criminal responsibility. Of course, that's what the Prosecution is supposed to do, to select facts to do that. Then object to it, therefore, if the facts in themselves are not in dispute seems to be a waste of time. And then to present evidence again on it seems to be a waste of time as well. It is a clear example of how we could do better, all of us, in this courtroom. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we are at 17 July, and are you aware of a series of intercepts with Colonel Popovic where he is intercepted reporting back about the various -- or about the job that he's doing over the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just give us a very brief overview of what you believe he is doing and we won't go, indeed, to those intercepts individually, they are already into evidence and there maybe some adjudicated facts in there but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, as various documents indicate, the engineer equipment of the Zvornik Brigade is being engaged in continuing to bury bodies with respect to those killed at not only Rocevic, Kozluk, but also in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engineer logbook for the Zvornik Brigade actually notes on day by day where engineer equipment is and in fact it corresponds to known grave sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Popovic is still up at -- in these locations, particularly Pilica, to ensure that that activity is completed. There are a series of intercepts, obviously, where people are talking back and forth either wanting to talk to Colonel Popovic or I believe in one case basically saying: Don't worry you don't need to come to the headquarters, stay up there until the job is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at one point does he report back and give the job he's doing a particular grade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he notes that the job was done to a grade A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was the burial job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that it's completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1499. This is a document I think you'd asked for earlier. It's the 18th July interim combat report from Vinko Pandurevic, where he talks about the losses from some of the time period that we have been talking about and some other time periods. Let's go to page 2 in the English, it should be B/C/S page 4. And looking down at the bottom of the English page, we see Pandurevic saying: "During the last 10 days or so, the municipality of Zvornik has been swamped with Srebrenica Turks. It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who have fled into the forest." What do you take of this? Is this something that you were referencing earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, going back, Colonel Pandurevic obviously understood the real purpose of why this commission of three officers was visiting Zvornik. And what this interim combat report is, when you look at it in its totality, is Colonel Pandurevic's written defence on many issues pertaining to his ability and competence to command and why he's made the decisions that he has. In this particular paragraph, he's noting two different groups of Muslims who were in the Zvornik municipality. I guess if you look at the next line or the next page in English where he talks about creating an extremely complex situation, he's correct. He distinguishes between the 7.000 individuals that he attributes to being part of the column, he also distinguishes between the 3.000 who are in the schools in his municipality as being separate from those in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These 3.000 in the schools he's referencing, do you believe, is that in any way related to the people he referenced in his 15 July interim combat report when he said the additional burden on us is -- are the Muslims in schools throughout the zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, were any of the Muslims held in the schools, did any of them escape execution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the investigation has borne out that four of the Muslims held in the school at Orahovac escaped execution, two from Petkovci, there were none that I'm aware of from Rocevic, and the total of seven from Branjevo although four were later recaptured and are now subsequently missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's the subject matter of some of your narrative, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in my narrative report, chapter 8 deals with the issues of individuals who by documentary evidence can be identified in the custody of the VRS at some point during July of 1995 and who are now correspondingly missing. In the -- I believe a year later, I produced an addendum, when additional documentary evidence became available that identified additional individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, of the four people that you know from the documents that escaped from Branjevo Farm but then were recaptured by the Zvornik Brigade, how were they used, if you recall, from the documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The documents that I reference in that part of my analysis, these four individuals sought shelter at the home of a group of Serbs. They were taken in. They were essentially given food and water. They left the home, moved out in a different direction and were later captured by Bosnian Serb forces. Statements were taken from those individuals, and ultimately their statements that were taken from them were used to -- used to initiate criminal charges against the two individuals who were Bosnian Serb soldiers who had given them aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those four Muslims that were used as witnesses, have they been seen or heard from since July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I included that information in my narrative, the last information that I had on them is that they were on the ICRC missing list. I've not heard any information since then that reflects that they may have been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I ask one question? Witness, in -- on page, the second page of this document in English, and I read from there: "It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who have fled into the forests." Now, how do you understand this to be inconceivable? Is it that someone has been so irresponsible for having detained 3.000 persons in schools or is it inconceivable that it happened or that the 3.000 were in addition to? What is in your view exactly inconceivable here, or how is it meant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back one page in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's under number 4, last few lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To answer your question, what I believe that Colonel Pandurevic is, of course, now complaining about is that the decision was made to bring them to the schools to the Zvornik Brigade. Obviously, his criticism comes in hindsight of what happened. As I've testified previously, the VRS did not have a clear picture to the size of the column or the military threat to Zvornik when this decision was made to essentially start moving these prisoners to schools in the Zvornik municipality. In fact, they thought it was a good idea at the time because these schools were located far from the front lines, in remote areas, and would be an ideal place to do that. Obviously, in retrospect, with the column emerging as the threat that it was, it turned out to be a very poor idea with respect to what happened in Zvornik during the subsequent days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's inconceivable that someone took this odd decision or that this line was taken, is that how to interpret it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, again he's -- after the fact he's complaining about the thought process of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I see that, but the inconceivable could relate to many parts of these observations, about numbers or whatever, but it is about the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my view, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's now go to 65 ter 4312. This is a 22 July document, another interim combat report from Vinko Pandurevic to the Drina Corps, and we can see that it's talking about engaging enemy groups along Planinci-Perunika-Brezik village line. Ten enemy soldiers were liquidated, armed mostly with weapons, automatic weapons, while 23 Muslim soldiers were captured. Just -- are there still, in your view, hundreds of Muslims in these woods around Zvornik along the path of the column and the other area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Once the 24-hour window for the column is expired and Colonel Pandurevic closes and resecures his lines, there are still hundreds of men, Bosnian Muslim men, soldiers, who are now still trapped in Bosnian Serb military territory. And as both police and military documents reflect, on the day of the 17th and the 18th, correspondingly through even into August, various military units are involved in sweeping the terrain in order to police all of these individuals up. Some are captured, some are killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether the word "liquidated" here, whether you understand that to be killed in a combat context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this particular time, I don't know that I could make that kind of distinction because, as I believe the Court is aware, from the results of the investigation, there were many cases where prisoners were taken immediately resulting from the combat and killed so it's just it's impossible to distinguish at this time. I would generally give it the more benign interpretation of their talking about legitimate combat operations but I'm aware that there is again information to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that regard, Mr. Butler, are you aware of a survivor of an execution near Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you aware of a survivor of an execution near Snagovo, around this time period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I'm also familiar with the Snagovo investigation. I think that parts of that occurred after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, does it make any sense from a military perspective, with Muslim -- armed Muslims, some of which would have automatic weapons, in the woods, does it make any sense on the time period of the 14th of July, after -- at the time executions began in Orahovac, through the 15th, 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th, up until even the 22nd here, does it make any sense militarily, during this very intense time that you've described, for the Zvornik Brigade's or the VRS to enlist any resources into going out into these woods and these battle areas to identify fallen Muslim soldiers and bring them back and put them in big unidentified graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not this early. I mean obviously at some point, fallen bodies on the battlefield, where they have fallen, close to or near Bosnian Serb military positions, would be policed up because of the health and biological hazard that they represent. But as evidenced by the larger body of information, there are still active combat operations that are occurring in these areas on these dates, so the retrieval or burial of dead enemy casualties would not be as high a priority, for example, as continuing to sweep the terrain for the purpose of liquidating armed enemy groups that are still operating behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Liquidating meaning killing in combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then number 3: "We request from the corps command that the exchange commission start work as soon as possible. We also require instructions as to what to do with the prisoners, where to put them, and whom we should hand them over." What's this "we also require instructions as to what to do with prisoners"? Vinko Pandurevic not know what to do with prisoners? What do you take of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, as the evidence has indicated and the military documents have indicated, Colonel Pandurevic, at least by 15 July 1995, is aware of thousands of prisoners in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. He is also aware that his units are engaged against the column and clearly would also understand that prisoners are being taken by Bosnian Serb military forces, by those fighting forces. He acknowledges on the 18th, 3.000 prisoners were in the custody of the Zvornik Brigade with respect to the schools that they are in. Only now on the 22nd of July, for the first time is there a reflection that there might be a change in the guidance from higher headquarters and we are not instantly killing prisoners as we encounter them anymore, and Colonel Pandurevic is asking, What would you like me to do with these prisoners that we are still taking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04312 receives number P2130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, are you aware of a series of intercepts beginning August 1st and going into August 2nd, sometimes involving Popovic, sometimes involving Krstic, sometimes involving Beara, and relating to Muslim men that have fled across the Drina at about that time period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Without going into each of those individually, can you just tell us what those intercepts told you? They are all in evidence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At that time, Bosnian Muslims from the Zepa enclave, many of them sought refuge in Serbia, and for whatever reason, the Serbian political and police authorities made a decision not to immediately turn those people back over to the custody of the Army of the Republika Srpska. The intercepts that are talked about and that Mr. McCloskey just referenced reflect the dissatisfaction of high-ranking individuals from the Drina Corps and the Main Staff to those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just in the end, those men from Zepa that, roughly how many, as far as the intercepts count, was, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the number at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know eventually what happened to them? Were they given back to RS or what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My understanding is that the ICRC in Serbia was given access to those prisoners and they were in fact registered. They were not turned over to the custody of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go briefly to P1500. This is a document that the Trial Chamber has seen before. It's dated September 14th in the name of General Mladic, and we see SR next to it in the Serbian, and it's approving five tonnes of diesel fuel for engineering works in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps to be delivered to the Standard barracks in Zvornik to Captain Milorad Trpic. What do you think this is about and who is Trpic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact it is Captain Milorad Trbic who is the deputy chief of security for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
